meta.title: Careers — The Engineering Guild & Incubator — MIW
meta.description: MIW takes ambitious first- and second-year developers, puts them on real enterprise work under Principal-level supervision, and pays a share of it. Three open directions, a published hiring process, and an application that asks for your work rather than your CV.

title: The MIW Engineering Guild
lede: We are not an outsourcing galley. We are an engineering laboratory: ambitious first- and second-year developers on real production work, under Principal-level supervision, paid a share of what it earns.
body: This is not an internship and it is not a course. You join a crew building a system that a paying client depends on, your work goes through the same review gate as everyone else's, and when the project earns money you earn a cut of it. The strongest work becomes a lab product with its builders on the cap table.

tracks.label: Real enterprise stack
tracks.body: Transactional booking platforms, payment pipelines and catalogue systems under real load — not a to-do app.

tracks.label: Principal-level mentorship
tracks.body: Weekly design review with the architect who owns the system, on the code you shipped that week.

tracks.label: Royalties, not a stipend
tracks.body: Revenue share on the commercial projects you build, paid when the studio is paid.

tracks.label: Co-founded startups
tracks.body: Lab products spun out with equity for the people who built them.

expectations: You already build things nobody asked you to build.
You can read a codebase you did not write without giving up.
You want the review that tells you what is wrong, not the one that says nice work.

readiness.label: The stack you would be dropped into
readiness.body: Go and Java on the service side, Next.js and TypeScript on the surface, Kubernetes underneath. You are not expected to arrive fluent in all of it — you are expected to be willing to be a beginner in public, weekly.

readiness.label: Event-driven thinking
readiness.body: Queues, retries, at-least-once delivery and what it costs. If the phrase 'this handler will be called twice' does not yet worry you, this is the part of the job that will teach you why it should.

readiness.label: Deterministic code
readiness.body: Same input, same output, same result on someone else's machine. Code whose behaviour depends on timing, ordering or a machine's local state is the thing the review gate exists to catch.

backend.label: Backend & Distributed Systems
backend.level: Open to first-year students through working engineers
backend.body: Services that hold under load, and transactions that hold under contention. You will work on locking, failure domains and deploy topology on a platform that is already serving requests.
work: Own an endpoint end to end: contract, transaction boundary, failure response, the runbook when it degrades.
Write the concurrent test that proves two requests for the last seat cannot both win, then make it pass.
Take a latency regression from the p99 chart down to the query that spent the budget.
backend.signal: Show us something concurrent you wrote and can explain the failure modes of.

commerce.label: Commerce, Payments & Throughput
commerce.level: Open to anyone who wants the hard part of a checkout, not the UI
commerce.body: Order pipelines built for the worst hour: idempotent payment handling, cache tiers, queued documents. This is also where our applied-AI work lands first, because an order pipeline is where automation has something measurable to do.
work: Make a webhook handler idempotent and prove it by replaying a real delivery twice.
Load-test the catalogue path and move the ceiling by a cache tier rather than by a bigger instance.
Move something slow off the checkout path onto a queue without losing the failure signal.
commerce.signal: Show us something you built that handles money, retries or both, and tell us what you got wrong first.

frontend.label: Modern Frontend & Systems UI
frontend.level: Open to anyone who can make a dense interface stay fast
frontend.body: Interfaces over large data sets and dense operational readouts. Performance is a requirement on this track, not a pass somebody does later.
work: Hold a route-change budget on a page rendering a catalogue, with the cache cold.
Cut hydration down to the surface that actually responds to a click, and measure the difference.
Make the accessible path the default one, not the retrofit.
frontend.signal: Show us an interface you built where the hard part was the data, not the styling.

01.label: Application
01.body: You link the thing you built and tell us what was hard about it. A Principal Architect reads it — there is no recruiter screen and no CV parser in front of them.

02.label: Code conversation
02.body: Forty-five minutes on your own code. Why it is shaped that way, what you tried that did not work, what you would change now. No whiteboard puzzles.

03.label: Paired change
03.body: A small real change to one of our systems, paired with the architect who owns it. You see the review gate from the inside before you commit to anything.

04.label: Crew placement
04.body: You join a crew with a named architect and a weekly design review. Revenue-share terms are in writing before your first commit, not after it.

paid.a: You get a revenue share on the commercial projects you build, paid when the studio is paid, and equity in lab products that spin out with you on them. It is not a stipend and it is not an unpaid internship.

experience.a: No. The filter is the work you link, not where it was written. Most of the intake is first- and second-year students who build things nobody asked them to build.

university.q: Can I do this alongside university?
university.a: The programme is designed around people who are still studying, so yes. Tell us your realistic hours in the application and we will build the crew around them rather than pretending they do not exist.

fit.q: None of the three directions fit me.
fit.a: These are directions, not headcount. Apply to the closest one and say so in the last field — a strong applicant gets a crew built around them.

after.a: A Principal Architect reads it and you get a written answer, usually inside a week. If it is a no, the answer says what would change it.

sections.openingsNote: These are directions, not headcount. We are not filling a seat with a fixed title — a strong applicant on any of them gets a crew built around them.
sections.hiringNote: Published because not knowing is what stops people applying. Every step is something we do to your work, not a personality screen.
